No, it is not. X (formerly Twitter) has kept the name X since the rebrand happened. There has been no official switch back to Twitter, and nothing suggests one is coming.

I get why people keep asking this. The rebrand was messy, confusing, and a lot of long term users never fully adjusted to it. Old habits stick, especially with a platform people used daily for over a decade.

But as it stands now, the name, the logo, and the branding are all X. If you are seeing anything that says otherwise, it is worth checking where that information came from.

The core function of the platform has not changed. You can still post short updates, follow accounts, reply, and share links. The basic structure that made Twitter useful is still there under the X name.

What changed was the branding. The blue bird logo was replaced with the X logo. The web address changed. The app icon changed. The company itself was restructured under X Corp.

None of that reversed. If you open the app today, you will still see X branding throughout, not Twitter branding.

2. Check the top of the app or website for the current logo.
3. Look at the web address bar when you visit the site.
4. Check your account settings page for the platform name listed there.

This takes less than a minute and gives you a clear, current answer rather than relying on memory or rumour.

title: Musk wins court order to block use of “Twitter,” but not “tweet” and bird logo - Ars Technica
text:
On Thursday, Elon Musk’s X won a court order blocking Operation Bluebird from launching a new app taking over the Twitter name.

In his opinion, Chief Judge Colm Connolly explained that Operation Bluebird was unlikely to prove that X had entirely abandoned the Twitter name. Therefore, X was likely to succeed on trademark infringement and dilution claims tied to the platform’s former name.

Most compellingly, X argued that it still uses the Twitter name in the current listing for the X app in Apple’s App Store. In the first sentence of that listing, written in the same size font as the rest of the text, a single clause clinched the early court win for X by stating, “Welcome to X (formerly known as Twitter).”

X’s legal director, Naser Baseer, testified that X “deliberately” added that clause “to ensure that people who were searching for the Twitter app within the App Store, as well as people who were searching for the Twitter app outside of the App Store, would find the Apple app link and have an understanding that this is one and the same app, same platform,” Connolly said.

Additionally, survey evidence showed that people still think Twitter’s a “famous” brand, and X showed that despite wiping the name from its platform, the company still “takes advantage” of the “goodwill” that the “commercially strong” initial brand maintains by associating X with Twitter in the App Store, Connolly wrote.

“By virtue of the parenthetical, the listing is telling customers that what they knew as Twitter is now X and can be accessed by downloading the X app from the Apple App Store,” Connolly said.

It may also strengthen X’s case that twitter.com redirects to x.com, but Connolly did not yet have to weigh that question. Because X could be irreparably harmed if Operation Bluebird benefits from using the Twitter name at X’s expense, Operation Bluebird will be blocked from using the name until litigation is resolved, Connolly ruled.

## X can’t block bird logo, “tweet” uses

However, X was not as successful in its claims that it had not abandoned other Twitter marks, including uses of the term “tweet” and the bird logo.

Musk’s public claims that “soon we shall bid adieu to the Twitter brand and, gradually, all the birds” and “we’re cutting the Twitter logo off the building with blow torches” provided “compelling evidence that X Corp. harbors an intent not to resume use of the Tweet mark and Bird logo,” the judge found. Therefore, Operation Bluebird is likely to prove that X abandoned those trademarks.

...

“The cited web pages are in short remnants of prior use of the Tweet mark and the Bird logo, not evidence that X Corp. is currently engaged in the bona fide use of those marks,” Connolly decided.

The same logic applies to legacy social media accounts X left up on the platform, including the deactivated account, @twitter, which tells people to “follow @x for updates.”

...

“For all these reasons, I find it likely that Bluebird will succeed in strictly proving that X Corp. has discontinued bona fide use of the Tweet mark and Bird logo,” Connolly wrote, denying X’s motion to block the uses.

## New Twitter quickly rebrands

In a press release provided to Ars, Operation Bluebird President Stephen Coates celebrated the outcome.

“They kept the word,” Coates said. “They let go of the bird, and they let go of the tweet.”

Durk Barnhill, Operation Bluebird’s chief marketing officer, told Ars that “we think this is a huge win” and confirmed that the rival app was immediately renamed following the court’s order.

Operation Bluebird had already launched a domain, twitter.new, but the August 26 launch was not mentioned as part of the court proceedings, so the judge did not directly discuss how his order might impact the rival service.

Despite the judge’s silence, Operation Bluebird has already rebranded, declaring in a press release that “Tweet.App” will be the platform’s new name.

Users unaware of the rebrand may experience issues accessing the new site, though. On early Thursday, Ars noted that twitter.new was redirecting to tweet.app, but, as of this writing, has reverted to a page that previously used the Twitter name to encourage users to sign up for handles. Barnhill confirmed that Operation Bluebird is working through bugs, so the redirect will likely be fixed soon.

Apart from the name of the app, nothing else has changed for the 172,000 users who have already requested handles, the press release said.

Operation Bluebird has launched a new website, Twitter.now, while its legal trademark battle with Elon Musk’s social media platform X over the former Twitter brand remains unresolved.

The launch follows Operation Bluebird’s efforts to claim trademark rights associated with the original Twitter identity. The organisation argues that X abandoned parts of the former Twitter branding after Musk renamed the platform in 2023.

...

The trademark dispute centres on whether X still holds rights to the Twitter name, the term “tweet” and the platform’s well-known blue bird logo.

A federal judge has tentatively questioned X’s rights to some of these trademarks. However, the court has not issued a final ruling, and the case remains active in federal court.

Operation Bluebird argues that X abandoned parts of the original Twitter identity when it replaced the Twitter name and bird branding with X.

However, X disputes these claims and continues to contest the trademark challenge.

#### Twitter.now Launches as Case Remains Pending

With Twitter.now now launched, Operation Bluebird is moving forward while the trademark dispute continues.

The launch does not mean that Operation Bluebird has won the rights to the original Twitter trademarks. The court still needs to resolve the dispute, and no final decision has established who can legally use the contested branding.

The outcome could determine the future ownership and use of the Twitter name, the word “tweet” and the platform’s iconic bird logo.

title: The Twitter brand is back. It's not how you remember it
text:
Twitter.now argues Elon Musk’s X abandoned the old Twitter brand, so it’s adopted the look—albeit with a twist.

September 1, 2026

[Illustration: FC]

BY Hunter Schwarz

Arguing that Elon Musk abandoned the old Twitter name and logo when he rebranded the social network to X, a group called Operation Bluebird has launched Twitter.now, an X alternative that brings back the Twitter branding and logo with a twist.

[Images: Twitter, Operation Bluebird]

The old Twitter logo was a blue bird called Larry, named after the Boston Celtics star Larry Bird, and its last iteration was released in 2012 and rendered using 13 overlapping circles. The logo for Twitter.now was designed differently, with feathers that flare out and suggest, perhaps, a phoenix rising from the ashes, but the colors and basic silhouette are still there. Its error page shows the bird on a dead whale, recalling the old Twitter’s “fail whale” graphic used during service outages. It also brings back Twitter’s iconic bright blue.

The site is selling early access starting at $20, and it states at the top of the page next to its logo that it’s “not affiliated with X Corp.” Still, it retains enough of the classic Twitter visual identity to evoke the old brand.

...

Operation Bluebird cofounder and former Twitter trademark counsel Stephen Coates wrote on LinkedIn that the site “is not an attempt to recreate the old platform.” While it has some of the same features as classic Twitter, such as handles, retweets, and replies, the creators emphasize a different kind of user experience that speaks to current frustrations some have with Musk’s X and social media today.

Operation Bluebird, which did not respond to a request for comment, contends X abandoned its trademarks.
